{{Short description|On centroids of sets of lattice points}}
In [[additive number theory]], '''Kemnitz's conjecture''' states that every set of [[integer lattice point]]s in the plane has a large [[subset]] whose [[centroid]] is also a lattice point. It was proved independently in the autumn of 2003 by [[Christian Reiher]], then an undergraduate student, and Carlos di Fiore, then a high school student.{{r|savchen}}

The exact formulation of this conjecture is as follows:

:Let <math>n</math> be a natural number and <math>S</math> a set of <math>4n-3</math> lattice points in plane. Then there exists a subset <math>S_1 \subseteq S</math> with <math>n</math> points such that the centroid of all points from <math>S_1</math> is also a lattice point.

Kemnitz's conjecture was formulated in 1983 by Arnfried Kemnitz{{r|kemnitz}} as a generalization of the [[Zero-sum problem|Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv theorem]], an analogous one-dimensional result stating that every <math>2n-1</math> integers have a subset of size <math>n</math> whose average is an integer.{{r|egz}} In 2000, Lajos Rónyai proved a weakened form of Kemnitz's conjecture for sets with <math>4n-2</math> lattice points.{{r|ronyai}} Then, in 2003, Christian Reiher proved the full conjecture using the [[Chevalley–Warning theorem]].{{r|reiher}}
